overview.text: Retroviruses are RNA-genome viruses distinguished by copying their genetic information into DNA after entering a cell, then inserting that DNA into the host’s genetic material. The enzyme reverse transcriptase makes the DNA copy; viral integrase helps insert it. Once integrated, the viral DNA can be used by the cell to make viral proteins and new virus particles. HIV is a well-known example and belongs to the lentiviruses, a subgroup of retroviruses. This replication strategy matters medically: some retroviruses are associated with serious diseases, including AIDS and some cancers.

key_facts.text: Reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy from the virus’s RNA; this RNA-to-DNA step is called reverse transcription.
Integration is a separate step: the viral enzyme integrase helps insert viral DNA into the host cell’s DNA.
After integration, HIV uses parts of its host CD4 cell to make viral proteins and new virus particles.
HIV belongs to the lentiviruses, a subgroup of retroviruses.
Retroviruses are associated with illnesses that include AIDS and some cancers.
